headline: High: pdf.js can feed unstructured’s writable, networked pipeline, creating default-path data leakage and cascading misprocessing risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: pdf.js ingests PDF files and runs browser-based tests, while unstructured reads documents and can write files. A prompt-injection path is plausible only if attacker-controlled PDF text is manually or programmatically passed from pdf.js into unstructured’s parsing pipeline; no shared channel is documented, so this stays low.
conditions: IF pdf.js output is copied into unstructured as document text or a generated file
IF a PDF contains attacker-controlled instructions that survive extraction and are later interpreted as directives
mitigations: Keep pdf.js and unstructured in separate workspaces
Strip instructions from extracted text before handing it to unstructured
Use a fixed schema for handoff files
Review a sample extracted document before batch processing

B_data_leakage.rationale: pdf.js handles PDF documents locally with no network egress, but unstructured can read files and has allowlisted network egress plus API calls. If the same documents are shared between them, unstructured may transmit document contents to its backend or APIs by default, creating a medium leakage path in default use.
conditions: IF the same sensitive PDF is processed by both agents in a shared workspace
IF unstructured sends document contents to its allowlisted endpoints during parsing
mitigations: Process sensitive PDFs only with pdf.js
Disable network access for unstructured on sensitive jobs
Use a redaction step before unstructured ingestion
Route unstructured to a local-only environment for test runs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: pdf.js supports multiple instances and works on PDF files, while unstructured can read and write the filesystem, install packages, and spawn subprocesses. Their overlapping document-processing role can conflict on shared files or outputs; the profiles do not show locking or isolation between them, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same document directory
IF unstructured modifies files that pdf.js is simultaneously reading or generating
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize writes with a simple operator-managed lock file
Make pdf.js outputs read-only before unstructured runs
Run one agent at a time on shared documents

D_cascading_error.rationale: pdf.js produces rendered or extracted PDF content, and unstructured is a document parser that can consume files and produce downstream outputs. Because no verification or provenance tracking is documented between them, unstructured may treat pdf.js-derived content as authoritative, causing cascading parsing or transformation errors.
conditions: IF unstructured consumes text or files produced by pdf.js without a validation step
IF downstream actions rely on unstructured output derived from pdf.js extraction
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents
Compare extracted text against the source PDF for a sample set
Attach provenance metadata to handoff files
Reject outputs that fail a simple checksum or row-count check

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source document-processing tools, but pdf.js is local-only with no egress while unstructured advertises allowlisted network calls and privacy-policy endpoints. The main compliance issue is a potential policy mismatch on document handling rather than a residency or regulated-data breach, so low fits.
conditions: IF regulated documents are sent through unstructured’s networked endpoints
IF the operator requires all document processing to remain local
mitigations: Keep regulated documents on pdf.js only
Review unstructured’s privacy policy before use
Disable network egress for compliance-sensitive runs
Document the approved data classes for each agent
